en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on the Pairs, 23. The Training Rule on Medicines.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Pilindavaccha was having a mountain slope cleared at Rājagaha, desiring to build a cave-dwelling.
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha approached the Venerable Pilindavaccha;
having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Pilindavaccha and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the King...
Seniya Bimbisāra of Māgadha said to the Venerable Pilindavaccha, “Venerable sir, what is the Elder having done?
“A mountain slope, great king; I am having it cleared, desiring to have a cave constructed.
“Does the noble one, venerable sir, require an attendant from the monastery?”
“Great King, the Blessed One has not yet authorized a monastery attendant.
“In that case, venerable sir, please ask the Blessed One and let me know,” [the king said].
“Yes, Great King,” the Venerable Pilindavaccha replied to Seniya Bimbisāra, the King of Magadha.

Then the Venerable Pilindavaccha instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha with a discourse on the Dhamma. Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired,
and gladdened by the Venerable Pilindavaccha with a discourse on the Dhamma, rose from his seat and [approached] the Venerable Pilindavaccha.
Having paid homage and circumambulated him, he departed.
Then the Venerable Pilindavaccha sent a messenger to the Blessed One, saying:
"Venerable sir, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha wishes to give an attendant to the monastery."
“Venerable sir, how should I proceed?
Then, on this occasion and in this context, the Blessed One gave a discourse on the Dhamma and addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, I allow you a monastery attendant.”
A second time, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha approached the Venerable Pilindavaccha;
having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Pilindavaccha, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha said this to the Venerable Pilindavaccha:
“Venerable sir, has the Blessed One permitted a monastery attendant?
“Yes, great king.
“In that case, venerable sir, I shall give a monastery attendant to the noble one.”
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, having promised a monastery attendant to the Venerable Pilindavaccha, forgot about it;
only after a long time did he regain his memory and address a certain high minister who was in charge of all affairs:
“Tell me, sir, did I promise a monastery attendant to the noble one? Was that attendant given?”
“Indeed, Your Majesty, no monastery attendant has been given to the noble one.
“How long, my man, has it been since then?
Then that chief minister, having counted the nights, said this to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha: “Five hundred nights, Your Majesty.”
“In that case, my good man, give five hundred monastery attendants to the noble one.

“Very well, Your Majesty,” the high minister replied to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, and he gave five hundred monastery attendants to the Venerable Pilindavaccha; a separate village was established for them.
They called it both Ārāmikagāmaka and Pilindagāmaka.
Now at that time, the Venerable Pilindavaccha was a regular visitor to the families in that village.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Pilindavaccha dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Pilindagāmaka for alms.
Now at that time, there was a festival in that village. The children were playing, adorned with ornaments and garlands.

Then the Venerable Pilindavaccha, while wandering for alms from house to house in Pilindagāma, approached the residence of a certain monastery attendant; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Now at that time, the daughter of that monastery attendant’s wife, seeing other children adorned with ornaments and garlands, began to weep, saying, “Give me a garland! Give me an ornament!”
Then the Venerable Pilindavaccha said this to that female monastery attendant: "Why is this girl crying?

"Venerable sir, having seen other girls adorned and garlanded, this girl cries out, 'Give me a garland! Give me an ornament! But from where would we, who are so poor, get a garland, from where an ornament?
Then the Venerable Pilindavaccha took a bundle of grass and said this to that female monastery attendant: "Well then, tie this bundle of grass on the head of that girl."
Then that park-keeper took that bundle of grass and tied it around the girl’s head. It became a golden garland—beautiful, lovely, and pleasing to behold.
There was no such golden garland even in the king’s inner apartments.
People reported this to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha: “Sire, in the house of a certain park-keeper there is a golden garland, beautiful, lovely, and pleasing to behold.”
“Even in the king’s inner palace there is no such golden garland;
how could that wretched man have it?
Without a doubt, it was brought by theft.”
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha had that family of monastery attendants bound.
A second time, the Venerable Pilindavaccha, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Pilinda Village for alms.

While walking for alms from house to house in Pilinda Village, he approached the residence of that monastery attendant; having arrived, he asked the neighbors, “Where has this family of monastery attendants gone?”
“Venerable sir, it was for the sake of that golden garland that the king had him imprisoned.
Then the Venerable Pilindavaccha went to the residence of Seniya Bimbisāra, the King of Magadha; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha approached the Venerable Pilindavaccha; having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Pilindavaccha, he sat down to one side.
As King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha was sitting to one side, the Venerable Pilindavaccha said to him: “Great King, why has the gardener’s family been imprisoned?
“Venerable sir, in that gardener’s house there is a golden garland that is beautiful, lovely, and pleasing.
There is no such golden garland even in our own inner palace.”
"How could that wretched man have it?
Without a doubt, it was brought by theft.
Then the Venerable Pilindavaccha resolved that the palace of King Seniya Bimbisāra of Māgadha was made of gold.
Thus it became entirely made of gold.
“But from where, Great King, did you obtain so much gold?
“It is known, Bhante; this is surely the power of the Noble One’s supernormal success.”
He had that family of park-keepers released.
People, hearing that “the noble Pilindavaccha has indeed displayed a superhuman feat of psychic power before the assembly including the king,” were delighted and full of faith;
they brought five kinds of medicinal tonics to the Venerable Pilindavaccha, namely: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses.
Moreover, by his very nature, the Venerable Pilindavaccha was a recipient of the five kinds of medicinal tonics.
Whatever he received, he would distribute to the community;
yet his community was characterized by abundance.
Whatever he received, he would collect and store it, filling jars and pots; he would also fill water-strainers and bags and hang them in the windows.
These remained there, hanging loose and disheveled. The dwellings became strewn and littered with rats.
When people wandering on a tour of the monasteries saw this, they complained, grumbled, and voiced their indignation:
“These recluses, sons of the Sakyan, are like private storekeepers, just like King Seniya Bimbisāra of Māgadha.
The bhikkhus heard those people grumbling, complaining, and spreading it about.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [and so on]... they grumbled, complained, and spread it about, saying:
“How indeed can monks consent to such abundance?
Then those monks, having rebuked them in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, monks, that monks consent to such abundance?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can those foolish men, monks, intend such abundance?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence … [and so on] … And thus,
monks, you should recite this training rule: ‘Now,
those medicines for sick monks that are to be consumed by licking, such as:’”
Ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses—having accepted these, they may be used after being stored for a maximum of seven days.
For one who exceeds that limit, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
Furthermore, those medicines which are to be taken as tonics by sick monks...
Ghee means cow-ghee, or goat-ghee, or buffalo-ghee; that is, the ghee of those whose meat is permitted.
Fresh butter means...
Butter is that very [product] of theirs.
Oil means sesame oil,
mustard seed oil, madhuka oil, castor oil, and fat oil.
"Madhu" means honey from bees.
"Phāṇitaṃ" means—
[It is] produced from sugarcane.
Having received them, they may be consumed as stored up for a maximum of seven days;
thus, they may be consumed for a maximum of seven days.
"For one who exceeds that limit, it becomes an offense of relinquishment (nissaggiya)" means that on the rising of the sun on the eighth day, it becomes an offense of relinquishment.
It must be relinquished to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to an individual.
And furthermore, monks, it should be relinquished in this way:
…pe… “Venerable sir, this medicine of mine, which has exceeded seven days, is to be relinquished.”
"I relinquish this to the Saṅgha" ...
"let him give it" ...
"let them give it" ... [and so on].
"I give it to the Venerable One.
If seven days have passed and he perceives that they have passed, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If seven days have passed and he is in doubt, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If seven days have passed and he perceives that they have not passed, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
If it has not been formally determined and he perceives that it has been determined, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If it has not been distributed and he perceives that it has been distributed, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If it has not been lost, but one perceives it as lost, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
If it has not been destroyed, but one perceives it as destroyed, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If it has not been burnt, but one perceives it as burnt, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If it is not stolen, but one perceives it as stolen, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
Having received back what was forfeited, it must not be used by means of physical consumption, nor swallowed;
rather, it should be applied to a lamp or to black pigment.
It should be used by another monk through physical enjoyment, not by being swallowed.
If seven days have not passed, but he perceives that they have passed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If seven days have not passed, but he is uncertain, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If seven days have not passed, and he perceives that they have not passed, there is no offense.
There is no offense if:
within the seven days he resolves [on another], gives it away, it is lost, it is destroyed, it is burnt, they take it after having snatched it away, or they take it on trust.
If one gives away what has been abandoned, vomited, or relinquished to one who is not fully ordained, and being without regard for it, receives it back and consumes it—
except in the case of one who is insane or an initial offender.
The third training rule on medicines is concluded.
